tools.name: vm_troubleshoot
tools.description: Diagnose KubeVirt VirtualMachine issues with automated root-cause detection. Collects VM status, VMI status, volumes, DataVolume/PVC state, cloud-init configuration, pod state, logs, and events, then runs heuristic checks to identify specific problems and suggest fixes. Returns a 'Detected Issues' section with CRITICAL/WARNING findings and actionable remediation steps, followed by raw diagnostic data. Use this tool FIRST whenever a user asks why a VM is not starting, stuck in Provisioning, crashlooping, failing to migrate, or exhibiting unexpected behavior. Automatically detects: missing StorageClasses, invalid PVC specs, dangerous cloud-init commands (shutdown/halt), nodeSelector migration blockers, failed migrations, and pod crashloops. If the user asks to fix or remediate the issue, use the Suggested Fixes from the report with vm_lifecycle (restart) or resources_create_or_update.

name.description: The name of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

namespace.description: The namespace of the VirtualMachine to troubleshoot

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort 80
  - Security config matches the stable deployment (no additional securityContext fields)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to target both deployments
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - Ports unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Pods:
  - Stable: 2 running (engine-v2-0 …)
  - Canary: 2 running (engine-v2-1 …)
- Endpoints for recommendation-engine now include 4 pod IPs (2 stable + 2 canary) on port 8080, which achieves ~50/50 traffic split.

Notes and next steps
- Traffic split is proportional to ready endpoints. Keeping both deployments at 2 replicas maintains ~50/50. Adjust replicas if you want to skew traffic (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Rollback to 100% stable quickly: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 or scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas.
- Monitoring suggestion: watch error rates/latency per version label (version=v2.0 vs v2.1) using your metrics/logs.

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  annotations:

  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort 80
  - Security config matches the stable deployment (no additional securityContext fields)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine to target both deployments
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
  - Ports unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Verification
- Pods:
  - Stable: 2 running (engine-v2-0 …)
  - Canary: 2 running (engine-v2-1 …)
- Endpoints for recommendation-engine now include 4 pod IPs (2 stable + 2 canary) on port 8080, which achieves ~50/50 traffic split.

Notes and next steps
- Traffic split is proportional to ready endpoints. Keeping both deployments at 2 replicas maintains ~50/50. Adjust replicas if you want to skew traffic (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Rollback to 100% stable quickly: update the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0 or scale engine-v2-1 to 0 replicas.
- Monitoring suggestion: watch error rates/latency per version label (version=v2.0 vs v2.1) using your metrics/logs.

I found the deployment failing due to an invalid image tag.

What I fixed:
- Root cause: Pod was in ImagePullBackOff because the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag does not exist.
- Change applied: Updated the image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest in Deployment debug/app.

Current status:
- Deployment debug/app: Available = True, Progressing = True
- Pod: 1/1 Running (e.g., app-7db8cc5485-qnrmm)

If you prefer a specific pinned version instead of latest (recommended for stability), tell me which tag to use and I’ll update it.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc" (event: ProvisioningFailed: storageclass.storage.k8s.io "sc" not found).
- Action taken: Created a StorageClass named "sc" using the minikube hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to create a PV and bind the PVC.
- Result:
  - PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, RWO) to PV pvc-e668860d-c318-4823-9b1c-43ed5b05b46e.
  - Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, podIP 10.244.0.43. Volume my-persistent-storage is mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html.

If you’d prefer to use your cluster’s default StorageClass (“standard”) instead of keeping “sc,” I can update the PVC accordingly (this may require recreating the PVC/PV and will delete the existing data in that volume unless we migrate it).

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but your Deployment probes and Service were using port 80 and custom paths (/get_status, /is_ready). That caused connection refused on health checks and the app wasn’t ready/available.

What I changed
- Deployment (orders/webapp):
  - Updated container to expose port 8080.
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Service (orders/webapp):
  - Updated targetPort to 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready and serving 200 OK on probes.
- Service points to the correct port (8080).
- No Ingress found in the orders namespace; the Service is ClusterIP (internal only).

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
- In-cluster test:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress/Route. Share the hostname you want to use.

Steps.message:
Checking if the pod is running and ready...
pod/webapp-7d8467cb84-8cqsm condition met
Success: Pod is now Ready
Current liveness probe path: /
Current readiness probe path: /
Success: Both probe paths have been fixed
Success: Pod is stable with acceptable number of restarts

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/pods. So “pod-reader” couldn’t list Pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant on the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no other changes were needed.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- Try listing pods with that SA:
  - kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you try -A (all namespaces), it will still be denied unless you bind a ClusterRole.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/pods. So “pod-reader” couldn’t list Pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant on the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no other changes were needed.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- Try listing pods with that SA:
  - kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Notes
- This permission is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you try -A (all namespaces), it will still be denied unless you bind a ClusterRole.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/pods. So “pod-reader” couldn’t list Pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to grant on the core API group:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no other changes were needed.

How to verify
- Check authorization:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods
- Try listing pods with that SA:
  - kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

- The Service selector didn’t match your Pods.
  - Service nginx had selector app=web.
  - Your Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx.
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.
- Also, the container (nginx-unprivileged) listens on 8080, while the Service’s targetPort was 80.

What I changed
- Updated Service web/nginx:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (name: http)
- Verified Endpoints now point to the Pod on port 8080.
- Validated in-cluster access: curl to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Current status
- web/nginx Service is healthy and reachable inside the cluster via:
  - DNS: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - ClusterIP: 10.99.85.51:80
- Your Deployment is running 1/1 and serving traffic.

If you need external access (from outside the cluster)
- There is no Ingress defined in namespace web.
- I can set up one of the following for you:
  - Ingress (recommended if you have an ingress controller)
  - Service type: LoadBalancer (cloud/provider dependent)
  - Service type: NodePort (simple, exposes a high port on each node)

- I left a temporary test pod (netshoot-test) in web for further checks. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Impact: Pods stayed Pending, so Service web-app-service had no (or incomplete) endpoints, causing connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local to be refused.

What I changed
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 replicas Available and Ready.
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-src7z: Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-tgwhk: Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now populated (example: 10.244.0.50:80, 10.244.0.51:80).
- Your frontend should now be able to connect to web-app-service.

Notes and options
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (you want these pods only on GPU/production nodes), you can:
  - Label the appropriate node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add the selector to the Deployment.
- Consider adding probes and pinning the image tag:
  - readinessProbe and livenessProbe on port 80 to improve reliability.
  - Use a fixed image tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) rather than latest for reproducibility.

Would you like me to:
- Reintroduce a controlled nodeSelector once nodes are labeled?
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment?
- Run a quick in-cluster connectivity test from a debug pod to confirm HTTP 200 from web-app-service?

- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app

  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app

      containers:

        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- Impact: Pods stayed Pending, so Service web-app-service had no (or incomplete) endpoints, causing connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local to be refused.

What I changed
- Removed the incompatible nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 replicas Available and Ready.
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-src7z: Running
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-tgwhk: Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now populated (example: 10.244.0.50:80, 10.244.0.51:80).
- Your frontend should now be able to connect to web-app-service.

Notes and options
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (you want these pods only on GPU/production nodes), you can:
  - Label the appropriate node(s): kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
  - Then re-add the selector to the Deployment.
- Consider adding probes and pinning the image tag:
  - readinessProbe and livenessProbe on port 80 to improve reliability.
  - Use a fixed image tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) rather than latest for reproducibility.

Would you like me to:
- Reintroduce a controlled nodeSelector once nodes are labeled?
- Add readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment?
- Run a quick in-cluster connectivity test from a debug pod to confirm HTTP 200 from web-app-service?

Here’s the current resource usage for the control-plane (master) nodes.

Discovery
- Control-plane nodes found: 1
  - mcp-eval-cluster (v1.35.1), 4 CPU cores, ~15.6 GiB RAM, Debian 12

Node mcp-eval-cluster usage (from kubelet Summary API)
- CPU
  - Instant usage: ~219m (0.219 cores) out of 4 cores ≈ 5.5% of node CPU
  - CPU pressure (PSI): some avg10 ≈ 1.07% (low), full ≈ 0.02% (very low)
- Memory
  - Usage: ~3.69 GiB (usageBytes)
  - Working set (hot memory): ~3.07 GiB
  - Available (free per Summary API): ~13.47 GiB
  - Allocatable capacity: ~15.6 GiB
  - Memory pressure: none
- Filesystem
  - Node filesystem used: ~70.3 GiB of 144.2 GiB (≈ 48.7% used, 51.3% free)
  - Image FS used: ~6.15 GiB (≈ 4.0% of capacity)
- PIDs
  - Processes: 1001 of 127,677 max (≈ 0.8%)
- Swap (host)
  - Total: ~3.17 GiB, in use: ~50.6 MiB
  - Pods: swap usage 0 (as expected)

Notable control-plane pod consumers (instantaneous)
- kube-apiserver: ~55–57m CPU, ~0.91 GiB working set
- etcd: ~28–29m CPU, ~0.11–0.14 GiB working set
- kube-controller-manager: ~10–13m CPU, ~0.10–0.11 GiB working set
- kube-scheduler: ~5–5.3m CPU, ~36–37 MiB working set
- KubeVirt operators/APIs present; the larger ones:
  - virt-operator: ~15m CPU, ~0.24–0.26 GiB working set
  - virt-api: ~0.86–0.89m CPU, ~0.15–0.16 GiB working set

Overall status
- The control-plane node has plenty of headroom: low CPU use (~5.5%), modest memory use (~3–4 GiB of ~15.6 GiB), no memory/IO pressure, and ~51% disk free.

Note
- The Metrics Server (kubectl top) is not available in this cluster; I used the kubelet Summary API and node capacity for these figures. If you want kubectl top outputs, I can install or guide installing Metrics Server.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the requested multi-tenant setup with namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies, following least-privilege and isolation requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user alice and ServiceAccount dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user bob and ServiceAccount dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user charlie and ServiceAccount dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-readers → ClusterRole view bound to users alice, bob, charlie and SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging and prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - staging: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters
  - prod: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access in dev-shared (via the RoleBindings above).

4) Resource Quotas
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace pod-to-pod traffic:
  - allow-ingress-from-self in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, staging, prod
- DNS egress for all namespaces above:
  - allow-dns-egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53)
- Developer namespace egress restricted to own namespace and dev-shared:
  - allow-egress-self-and-dev-shared in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared ingress allowed only from dev namespaces:
  - dev-shared-allow-ingress-from-dev (from namespaces labeled env=dev)
- Isolation between dev and staging/prod:
  - No policies allow dev → staging/prod or staging/prod → dev; default-deny ensures isolation (outside of DNS).

Notes and next steps
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- On some CNI providers, replies to allowed ingress are stateful; if you need to ensure responses from dev-shared to dev are explicitly permitted even with strict egress controls, I can add a minimal egress policy in dev-shared back to env=dev.
- If you prefer developers to have “edit” instead of “admin” in their own namespaces (to avoid RBAC administration within the namespace), say the word and I’ll recreate those RoleBindings accordingly.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated manifest for version control.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested multi-tenant setup with namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies, following least-privilege and isolation requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user alice and ServiceAccount dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user bob and ServiceAccount dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user charlie and ServiceAccount dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-readers → ClusterRole view bound to users alice, bob, charlie and SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging and prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - staging: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters
  - prod: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access in dev-shared (via the RoleBindings above).

4) Resource Quotas
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace pod-to-pod traffic:
  - allow-ingress-from-self in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, staging, prod
- DNS egress for all namespaces above:
  - allow-dns-egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53)
- Developer namespace egress restricted to own namespace and dev-shared:
  - allow-egress-self-and-dev-shared in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared ingress allowed only from dev namespaces:
  - dev-shared-allow-ingress-from-dev (from namespaces labeled env=dev)
- Isolation between dev and staging/prod:
  - No policies allow dev → staging/prod or staging/prod → dev; default-deny ensures isolation (outside of DNS).

Notes and next steps
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- On some CNI providers, replies to allowed ingress are stateful; if you need to ensure responses from dev-shared to dev are explicitly permitted even with strict egress controls, I can add a minimal egress policy in dev-shared back to env=dev.
- If you prefer developers to have “edit” instead of “admin” in their own namespaces (to avoid RBAC administration within the namespace), say the word and I’ll recreate those RoleBindings accordingly.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated manifest for version control.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the requested multi-tenant setup with namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies, following least-privilege and isolation requirements.

What’s in place

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- Full access to own namespace:
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user alice and ServiceAccount dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user bob and ServiceAccount dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-admin → ClusterRole admin bound to user charlie and ServiceAccount dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-shared-readers → ClusterRole view bound to users alice, bob, charlie and SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging and prod restricted to cluster admins only:
  - staging: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters
  - prod: RoleBinding admins-only → ClusterRole admin bound to Group system:masters

3) Service Accounts
- alice-sa in dev-alice
- bob-sa in dev-bob
- charlie-sa in dev-charlie
Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only access in dev-shared (via the RoleBindings above).

4) Resource Quotas
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu: 4
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - requests.memory: 8Gi
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - requests.cpu: 8
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - requests.memory: 16Gi
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

5) Network Policies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces:
  - dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace pod-to-pod traffic:
  - allow-ingress-from-self in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, staging, prod
- DNS egress for all namespaces above:
  - allow-dns-egress to kube-system/coredns (UDP/TCP 53)
- Developer namespace egress restricted to own namespace and dev-shared:
  - allow-egress-self-and-dev-shared in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared ingress allowed only from dev namespaces:
  - dev-shared-allow-ingress-from-dev (from namespaces labeled env=dev)
- Isolation between dev and staging/prod:
  - No policies allow dev → staging/prod or staging/prod → dev; default-deny ensures isolation (outside of DNS).

Notes and next steps
- Service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- On some CNI providers, replies to allowed ingress are stateful; if you need to ensure responses from dev-shared to dev are explicitly permitted even with strict egress controls, I can add a minimal egress policy in dev-shared back to env=dev.
- If you prefer developers to have “edit” instead of “admin” in their own namespaces (to avoid RBAC administration within the namespace), say the word and I’ll recreate those RoleBindings accordingly.

If you’d like, I can export a single consolidated manifest for version control.

What I set up
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db
  - 3 replicas initially
  - Each pod mounts a 1Gi PVC at /data (volumeClaimTemplates: data)
  - Init container writes the file /data/test with the content initial_data on first run
  - Main container runs busybox and sleeps
- Scaled StatefulSet db down to 1 replica

Notes
- The PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained when scaling down; if you scale back up later, those pods will reattach their original volumes with the seeded data.

How to verify quickly
- Check the remaining pod and file:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- cat /data/test  (expect: initial_data)

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and fixed using the vm-troubleshoot tool.

Root cause
- The VM’s spec includes a cloudInitNoCloud volume referencing Secret vm-cloud-init, but that Secret did not exist in the vm-test-troubleshoot namespace.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot:
  - Pod event: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
  - virt-launcher pod stuck Pending/PodInitializing and VM Ready=False (GuestNotRunning)

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal cloud-init content (both userData/userdata and networkdata keys provided for compatibility).
- Restarted the VirtualMachine to pick up the new Secret.

Verification and outcome
- After the fix and restart:
  - VM status: printableStatus=Running, Ready=True
  - VMI phase: Running
  - virt-launcher pod: virt-launcher-broken-vm-glp7w is Running (2/2), on node mcp-eval-cluster
  - IP assigned to VMI: 10.244.0.86
  - Events confirm VirtualMachineInstance created and started successfully
- Note: There was a brief transition where the VM controller reported a start failure/CrashLoopBackOff while reconciling prior failures, but after the restart it stabilized and is now running normally.

If you want different cloud-init content (e.g., users, SSH keys, packages), I can update the vm-cloud-init Secret accordingly and recycle the VM.

Steps.message: VM created with missing Secret reference - waiting for failure state

Here’s what I found and fixed using the vm-troubleshoot tool.

Root cause
- The VM’s spec includes a cloudInitNoCloud volume referencing Secret vm-cloud-init, but that Secret did not exist in the vm-test-troubleshoot namespace.
- Evidence from vm-troubleshoot:
  - Pod event: MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "cloudinit-udata": secret "vm-cloud-init" not found
  - virt-launcher pod stuck Pending/PodInitializing and VM Ready=False (GuestNotRunning)

Action taken
- Created the missing Secret vm-cloud-init in vm-test-troubleshoot with minimal cloud-init content (both userData/userdata and networkdata keys provided for compatibility).
- Restarted the VirtualMachine to pick up the new Secret.

Verification and outcome
- After the fix and restart:
  - VM status: printableStatus=Running, Ready=True
  - VMI phase: Running
  - virt-launcher pod: virt-launcher-broken-vm-glp7w is Running (2/2), on node mcp-eval-cluster
  - IP assigned to VMI: 10.244.0.86
  - Events confirm VirtualMachineInstance created and started successfully
- Note: There was a brief transition where the VM controller reported a start failure/CrashLoopBackOff while reconciling prior failures, but after the restart it stabilized and is now running normally.

If you want different cloud-init content (e.g., users, SSH keys, packages), I can update the vm-cloud-init Secret accordingly and recycle the VM.

Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm.

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData runs a shutdown on first boot. When the guest powers off, KubeVirt immediately starts it again (because runStrategy=Always), causing an endless restart loop.

Cloud-init command causing the crashloop
- In cloud-init userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
Choose one of the following, depending on your intent:

- If you want the VM to stay up after initialization:
  - Remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData (runcmd). Example userData:
    #cloud-config
    runcmd: []
  - If you intended to apply changes and reboot once, replace the shutdown with cloud-init’s power_state module so the VM reboots but stays running:
    #cloud-config
    power_state:
      mode: reboot
      timeout: 30
      message: "Rebooting after cloud-init"
      condition: True

- If the VM is supposed to shut down after it finishes its work:
  - Keep the shutdown in cloud-init, but change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so KubeVirt does not auto-restart it.
    spec.runStrategy: Manual
  - Start it manually when you need it to run.

After updating the manifest (remove/adjust the shutdown or change runStrategy), restart the VM once to pick up the new configuration.

Steps.message: Waiting for VM to attempt boot and crash...

Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm.

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData runs a shutdown on first boot. When the guest powers off, KubeVirt immediately starts it again (because runStrategy=Always), causing an endless restart loop.

Cloud-init command causing the crashloop
- In cloud-init userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
Choose one of the following, depending on your intent:

- If you want the VM to stay up after initialization:
  - Remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData (runcmd). Example userData:
    #cloud-config
    runcmd: []
  - If you intended to apply changes and reboot once, replace the shutdown with cloud-init’s power_state module so the VM reboots but stays running:
    #cloud-config
    power_state:
      mode: reboot
      timeout: 30
      message: "Rebooting after cloud-init"
      condition: True

- If the VM is supposed to shut down after it finishes its work:
  - Keep the shutdown in cloud-init, but change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so KubeVirt does not auto-restart it.
    spec.runStrategy: Manual
  - Start it manually when you need it to run.

After updating the manifest (remove/adjust the shutdown or change runStrategy), restart the VM once to pick up the new configuration.

## Detected Issues

- **CRITICAL**: Cloud-init userData contains "shutdown" command that will shut down or restart the guest immediately after boot. Combined with runStrategy Always, this causes a crashloop.

## Suggested Fixes

1. Remove the "shutdown" command from cloud-init userData, or change runStrategy to Manual/Halted if the shutdown is intentional.

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found for vm-test-troubleshoot-ci/crashloop-vm.

Root cause
- The VM is configured with runStrategy: Always and its cloud-init userData runs a shutdown on first boot. When the guest powers off, KubeVirt immediately starts it again (because runStrategy=Always), causing an endless restart loop.

Cloud-init command causing the crashloop
- In cloud-init userData (cloudInitNoCloud), runcmd contains:
  - shutdown -h now

How to fix it
Choose one of the following, depending on your intent:

- If you want the VM to stay up after initialization:
  - Remove the shutdown line from cloud-init userData (runcmd). Example userData:
    #cloud-config
    runcmd: []
  - If you intended to apply changes and reboot once, replace the shutdown with cloud-init’s power_state module so the VM reboots but stays running:
    #cloud-config
    power_state:
      mode: reboot
      timeout: 30
      message: "Rebooting after cloud-init"
      condition: True

- If the VM is supposed to shut down after it finishes its work:
  - Keep the shutdown in cloud-init, but change the VM’s runStrategy to Manual or Halted so KubeVirt does not auto-restart it.
    spec.runStrategy: Manual
  - Start it manually when you need it to run.

After updating the manifest (remove/adjust the shutdown or change runStrategy), restart the VM once to pick up the new configuration.

results.taskOutput:
I attempted to retrieve guest agent data from VM test-vm-with-agent in namespace vm-test-guest-info, but the guest agent is not responding yet. The API returned:
- guestOSInfo/filesystems/users/networkInterfaces: VMI does not have guest agent connected

This usually means cloud-init is still running, the qemu-guest-agent service hasn’t started yet inside the guest, or the VM isn’t exposing the guest-agent virtio-serial channel.

What guest agent data typically includes (once it connects)
- OS
  - Pretty name and distribution (e.g., Fedora 39, Ubuntu 22.04)
  - Version and build
  - Kernel release/version
  - Architecture (x86_64, aarch64)
  - Hostname
  - Uptime and boot time
  - Timezone
- Filesystems
  - For each mounted filesystem: device, mount point, filesystem type (ext4, xfs), total size, used, available
  - Inode usage (used/free) per mount
- Network interfaces
  - Interface name (e.g., eth0, ens3)
  - MAC address
  - IP addresses (IPv4/IPv6)
  - Link state (up/down), MTU
- Logged-in users
  - Username
  - TTY/terminal
  - Source host (if remote)
  - Login time

If you want, I can retry in a bit and pull the live data as soon as the agent connects. If it keeps failing, likely next checks inside the guest are:
- Verify the service is running: qemu-guest-agent (systemd) is active and enabled.
- Ensure the VM spec includes the guest agent channel (target name org.qemu.guest_agent.0).
